what_its_for: Oxacillin is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections caused by certain types of bacteria called staphylococci (staph). It is commonly used for skin infections, bone infections, heart valve infections, and other serious infections. It works by stopping bacteria from building their protective outer wall, which kills them.
how_to_take: Oxacillin is usually given as an injection or IV (into a vein) in a hospital or clinic setting by a healthcare professional. If you are sent home with IV oxacillin, a nurse or doctor will show you exactly how to use it. Take it exactly as your doctor prescribes, at evenly spaced times throughout the day to keep a steady amount in your body. Do not skip doses, even if you start feeling better. Finish the full course of treatment.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose based on your weight, age, the type of infection, and how serious it is. Typical adult doses range from 250 mg to 2 grams every 4 to 6 hours. For children, the dose is based on body weight. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store oxacillin powder or solution as directed by your pharmacist or home health nurse. Reconstituted (mixed) solutions are typically stored in the refrigerator and used within 3 days, or kept at room temperature for up to 24 hours, but always follow the specific instructions on your label. Keep all medications out of reach of children. Do not freeze unless directed. Throw away any unused or expired medication properly.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking oxacillin with food or milk if given by mouth, as food can reduce how well it is absorbed — take it on an empty stomach at least 30 minutes before or 2 hours after eating. Avoid drinking alcohol during treatment, as it can affect your recovery. Do not take other antibiotics or medications without first checking with your doctor or pharmacist. Avoid taking antacids or supplements close to the time of your dose without guidance.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: a severe allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing; severe diarrhea or stomach cramps (which could be a sign of a serious gut infection called C. difficile); yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); dark urine; unusual bruising or bleeding; signs of kidney problems such as changes in how much urine you produce; or if your infection does not seem to be getting better after a few days.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within a few days of starting oxacillin, but it is very important to finish the entire course of treatment even if you feel well. Stopping early can allow the bacteria to come back and become harder to treat. Serious infections like bone or heart infections may take several weeks of treatment before you notice full improvement.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Oxacillin is generally considered safe during pregnancy when needed, but tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It can pass into breast milk in small amounts, so talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney or Liver Problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have kidney or liver disease. Elderly Patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects and should be monitored closely. Children: Oxacillin can be used in children; the dose will be carefully calculated based on weight. Penicillin Allergy: Do NOT take oxacillin if you are allergic to penicillin or any penicillin-type antibiotic. Tell your doctor about all your allergies before starting this medication.
